definition: Dendral was a project in artificial intelligence (AI) of the 1960s, and the computer software expert system that it produced.
details: Its primary aim was to study hypothesis formation and discovery in science. For that, a specific task in science was chosen: help organic chemists in identifying unknown organic molecules, by analyzing their mass spectra and using knowledge of chemistry. It was done at Stanford University by Edward Feigenbaum, Bruce G. Buchanan, Joshua Lederberg, and Carl Djerassi, along with a team of highly creative research associates and students. It began in 1964 and spans approximately half the history of AI research. The software program Dendral is considered the first expert system because it automated the decision-making process and problem-solving behavior of organic chemists. The project consisted of research on two main programs Heuristic Dendral and Meta-Dendral, and several sub-programs. It was written in the Lisp programming language, which was considered the language of AI because of its flexibility. Many systems were derived from Dendral, including MYCIN, MOLGEN, PROSPECTOR, XCON, and STEAMER. explainer.lead: Dendral was a Stanford AI project, begun in 1964, that produced software to help organic chemists identify unknown molecules from their mass spectra. It is considered the first expert system because it automated aspects of specialists' decision-making and problem-solving.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to identify a mystery substance from a pattern of clues, like solving a puzzle with a chemistry rule book. Dendral used a computer to combine those clues with chemistry knowledge and suggest what the substance might be. It helped chemists rather than trying to solve every kind of scientific problem.
tiers.practitioner: Dendral applied encoded chemistry knowledge to mass-spectral data to form hypotheses about unknown organic molecules. Written in Lisp, it comprised the main programs Heuristic Dendral and Meta-Dendral plus several sub-programs. Its scope was deliberately narrow: it supported organic chemists rather than providing a general-purpose scientific discovery system.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, Dendral mapped mass-spectral evidence together with chemistry knowledge to hypotheses about the identity of an unknown organic molecule. The project began at Stanford University in 1964 under Edward Feigenbaum, Bruce G. Buchanan, Joshua Lederberg, and Carl Djerassi, with research associates and students. Its central research aim was hypothesis formation and discovery in science, pursued through this specialized chemical task.

explainer.example: An organic chemist has an unknown organic sample and obtains its mass spectrum. Dendral analyzes that spectrum using chemistry knowledge and develops hypotheses about the molecule's identity, giving the chemist computer-assisted guidance rather than an unaided reading of the data.

explainer.intuition: A mass spectrum offers clues about an unknown molecule, but interpreting those clues requires specialist knowledge. Dendral's idea was to capture some of that expertise in software so the computer could help form and evaluate chemical hypotheses.
howItWorks: Start with the mass spectrum of an unknown organic molecule.
Analyze the spectrum as evidence about the sample.
Apply knowledge of chemistry to that evidence.
Form hypotheses about the molecule's identity to assist the organic chemist.
explainer.whyItMatters: Dendral showed that software could automate parts of a specialist's decision-making and problem-solving in a demanding scientific domain. It is therefore considered the first expert system, and its descendants included MYCIN, MOLGEN, PROSPECTOR, XCON, and STEAMER.
misconceptions: Dendral was not a single, general-purpose program: the project included Heuristic Dendral, Meta-Dendral, and several sub-programs.
It did not attempt all scientific discovery; its concrete task was identifying unknown organic molecules from mass spectra.
Modern programs for the mass spectrometry inverse problem are no longer generally described as artificial intelligence merely because they address the same task.
